name: Edge / CDN per-customer rate-limit & usage features
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Edge / CDN / serverless-edge per-customer rate-limit, quota and usage-metering counter store
domain_fit.one_line_definition: An edge / CDN / serverless platform-engineering team needs to decide on every inbound request — within a sub-millisecond budget shared with TLS termination and routing — whether a given (customer, API key, IP, route) is over a rolling rate / quota / token-bucket limit, and to keep a per-customer usage counter accurate enough to feed billing.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Enforce per-API-key / per-customer rolling rate limits (requests-per-second / per-minute / per-day) on every edge request before the request reaches origin or a serverless function, returning 429 with X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After headers. 2) Maintain per-customer usage counters (requests, bytes egressed, LLM tokens consumed, function-invocations, compute-ms) with windowing semantics that feed a usage-based billing pipeline (OpenMeter / Lago / Stripe Meters) without losing or double-counting events. 3) Provide a uniform 'counters + windows + token-bucket / GCRA / sliding-window' primitive across many edge platforms (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Netlify Edge Functions, Vercel Edge / Edge Config, Deno Deploy, Supabase Edge Functions) so platform teams stop writing bespoke Lua-on-Redis or Durable-Object code per provider.
domain_fit.event_shapes: request_observed {ts, edge_pop, customer_id, api_key, route, method, status, bytes_in, bytes_out, cpu_ms, region, ip, ua_hash}, function_invocation {ts, customer_id, function_id, duration_ms, memory_mb, cold_start, region}, llm_call {ts, customer_id, virtual_key, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens}, abuse_signal {ts, ip, customer_id, signal_type, score}, quota_consume {ts, customer_id, units, dimension}, kv_op {ts, customer_id, op, namespace, key_hash, size}. Beava's `@bv.event` declaration shape and HTTP/JSON :8080 plus framed TCP+msgpack :8081 push surfaces map directly onto how an edge worker emits these per-request events on a sidecar push.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Rate-limit side (token-bucket / sliding-window / GCRA primitives over count): count(request) per api_key in 1 s / 10 s / 60 s sliding windows; velocity(request) per (customer × route); count(429) per ip in 60 s; token_bucket(api_key, rate, burst) returning remaining and retry-after. Usage / billing side (counter / sum primitives): sum(bytes_out) per customer per hour / day / billing-period tumbling windows; sum(cpu_ms) per customer per day; sum(total_tokens) per (customer × model) per day; count(function_invocation) per customer per day. Abuse / DDoS side (velocity / distribution / n_unique primitives): velocity(request) per ip in 1 s / 10 s; n_unique(ip) per customer per 60 s (HLL acceptable); distribution(latency) per route per 60 s for SLO alerting.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite, with several natural keys depending on the rule: api_key, customer_id / tenant_id, ip address, (ip × route), (customer × route), (customer × model) for LLM-gateway use, virtual_key for AI-gateway sub-keys, function_id, edge_pop_id for per-POP local counters. Most production rules combine 2-3 of these into a composite key (e.g. (customer_id × route × method)).
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Both sliding and tumbling. Sliding-window (or GCRA / token-bucket which is effectively a sliding semantic) dominates for the rate-limit path because clients legitimately complain that fixed windows allow 2x-burst at boundaries. Tumbling windows dominate on the usage / billing side because Stripe / Lago / OpenMeter expect minute-aligned or hour-aligned buckets. Approximate aggregates are acceptable on the abuse side (HLL for n_unique IPs, CMS for top-talkers); EXACT counts are required on the per-customer billing side (sum of bytes / tokens that go into an invoice) and strongly preferred on the rate-limit side (especially when the rate-limit decision feeds 429 SLAs in a paid SLA tier). Cloudflare's published edge rate-limiting architecture explicitly trades exactness for per-PoP isolation and converges across PoPs asynchronously; Fastly's ratecounter computes RPS over 1 s / 10 s / 60 s windows with cross-cache-node convergence; both validate the 'per-region counter, eventually-consistent across regions' design point.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Bimodal. Rate-limit decisions tolerate at-least-once and minor over-count (and edge systems explicitly accept the risk of letting through a few extra requests during a partition); usage-metering for billing is strict no-double-count because the counter directly feeds an invoice (OpenMeter / Lago / Stripe Meters all use event-id-based dedup). The billing side is the harder semantic and is the side beava has to ship dedup-by-event-id for.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Sub-millisecond is the target for the inline rate-limit read. The whole edge request budget is typically 5-20 ms end-to-end including TLS / routing / origin; the rate-limit lookup must fit inside ~1 ms so Cloudflare advertises that its native Workers Rate Limiting API adds 'no meaningful latency'. Beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get sits inside the budget when co-located in the same PoP / availability zone; cross-region calls do not fit.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Single-digit seconds across regions, sub-second within a region. Cloudflare explicitly designs for per-PoP isolation with async convergence; Fastly's ratecounter converges across cache nodes in seconds. Billing-side counters tolerate minute-level freshness because OpenMeter / Lago pre-aggregate into 1-minute tumbling windows. Beava's push-on-event model gives sub-second within-region freshness directly.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Wildly bimodal. Cloudflare publicly handles tens of millions of requests/second globally across hundreds of PoPs; Fastly aggregate is in the millions of RPS; AWS API Gateway default per-account quota is 10,000 RPS with 5,000 burst. Per-PoP / per-region single-binary scope: a regional API gateway or a mid-size SaaS edge tier sits in the 10 k - 200 k RPS range, which one beava box at the published ~684 k EPS handles comfortably. Per-customer/tenant: an individual Cloudflare Durable Object is rated at ~500-1,000 RPS sustained — beava handles all customers on one box up to its global ceiling. Tier-1 CDN aggregate (Cloudflare/Fastly/Akamai global) does NOT fit one beava box and would require per-PoP deployment with cross-PoP async sync that beava v0 does not ship. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Roughly 1:1 on the rate-limit path (every request both reads the counter and increments it), shifting to write-heavy on the pure usage-metering path (one write per request, reads only at billing-aggregation cadence). Token-bucket / GCRA implementations typically fold read + write into a single atomic op, which suits beava's per-event push-and-track model.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by (customer × route × window) cardinality plus IP-keyed abuse counters. A mid-size SaaS with 100 k API customers × 50 routes × 3 windows => ~15 M counter cells × ~40-80 B each => ~600 MB - 1.2 GB hot state. An edge CDN serving millions of customer domains × tens of rules each (Cloudflare's blog explicitly addresses 'millions of domains × even more millions of rules') is 10^8 - 10^9 cells => 5-100 GB hot state, which fits one beava box but pushes the upper bound; the IP-keyed abuse side is explosive (10^7 - 10^9 unique IPs over a day) and is where eviction / TTL pressure lands. Aerospike, Redis-cluster, Memcached-via-Twemproxy and bespoke in-Rust per-PoP counters are the incumbents at this scale. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Bounded on routes / functions / models (10^2 - 10^4). Slowly growing on customers / api_keys (10^4 - 10^7). Explosive on IPs and (customer × ip) pairs (10^7 - 10^10 over a day). Drives memory budget and forces TTL / LFU eviction on the IP-keyed dimensions; Fastly's ratecounter explicitly caps at 200 000 entries per site with LRU eviction, which is the kind of constraint beava would need a primitive for.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Seconds to billing-period. Rate-limit counters: 1 s / 10 s / 60 s rolling windows, evictable after window expiry. Abuse / DDoS counters: 60 s - 24 h. Daily quotas: 24 h, midnight reset in customer's billing timezone. Monthly billing meters: 30 d with explicit period boundaries (OpenMeter / Lago / Stripe expect month-aligned). Long-lived state is the billing meter; short-lived is the per-IP abuse counter — TTL and eviction policy per dimension are the design pressure here.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 3-10 features per inline rate-limit check (per-API-key count, per-IP count, per-route count, current token-bucket balance, current quota balance, last-429-time). 1-5 features on the pure billing-read path (read aggregated meter for invoice generation). Lower than fraud's 20-100, but batch_get is still the natural shape because Cloudflare-style stacks evaluate multiple rules in parallel.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe for the rate-limit side (a node restart that drops the in-flight 60 s window is acceptable; clients will retry and the system will warm up again — Cloudflare's published design explicitly accepts per-PoP isolation and convergence failure as preferable to global blocking). Billing-grade durability is REQUIRED on the usage-metering side because the counter feeds an invoice and undercount means revenue leak / overcount means refund liability — this is the OpenMeter / Lago / Stripe-Meters design point and they use Kafka + ClickHouse explicitly for at-least-once with event-id dedup. beava's WAL + periodic snapshot is the right shape for the rate-limit side; the billing side needs first-class idempotency-by-event-id which beava does not document as a primitive in v0. [uncertain]
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Strong fit for single-binary per region / per PoP, which is exactly how Cloudflare runs (each PoP isolates a counting system internally and converges async — see 'Counting Things — a lot of different things'), how Fastly runs (per-cache-node ratecounter that converges within a site), and how Kong / Tyk / NVIDIA-go-ratelimit / Gubernator deploy. Beava's 'single-binary, refuse-on-network-FS, in-memory + WAL on local NVMe' rule is exactly what an edge-companion sidecar should look like. The misfit is multi-region / global-consistent counters — beava v0 cannot do cross-region active-active counter merge, so any rule that needs a single global cap (e.g. 'no customer can exceed 10 M requests/day globally') has to be approximated via per-region budgets that sum to the global limit, which is the same compromise Tyk DRL and Fastly's ratecounter already make.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Platform-as-a-service / edge-runtime / API-gateway engineering teams: (a) edge runtime providers (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Netlify Edge, Vercel Edge / Edge Config, Deno Deploy, Supabase Edge Functions, Bun's upcoming edge tier), (b) API-gateway vendors (Kong, Tyk, Apigee, Zuplo, Apache APISIX, Solo Gloo, Envoy Gateway), (c) AI / LLM gateway teams (Portkey, Helicone, LiteLLM, TrueFoundry, Cloudflare AI Gateway, AWS Bedrock Gateway, Envoy AI Gateway, Kong AI Rate Limiting), (d) self-hosted-platform engineers building bespoke internal-developer-platform gateways at large enterprises, (e) usage-based-billing platform teams that ship an edge-companion meter (OpenMeter, Lago, Metronome, Orb, Schematic, Stripe Meters integrators). Not the application developer — the platform-team operator who runs the gateway as a multi-tenant service.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Large and growing. API management market is $5.7B (2023) -> ~$15B by 2030 (Grand View / Gartner adjacent numbers). Edge-compute market broadly tracked at $11-15B in 2024 with 30 %+ CAGR to ~$60B by 2030. Usage-based-billing software (OpenMeter, Lago, Metronome, Orb, Stripe Meters) is in the early-but-fast-growth phase — Stripe publicly positions usage-based billing as the dominant model for AI / SaaS in 2025-2026 and OpenMeter publicly claims processing of 'millions of usage events per minute'. AI-gateway is a brand-new ~2024-2026 category with Portkey, Helicone, LiteLLM and TrueFoundry all explicitly anchored on per-customer token-counter rate-limiting and metering. The Cloudflare blog 'Counting Things — a lot of different things' is direct evidence that the cost of running rate-limit counter state at edge scale is large enough that the largest CDN in the world wrote a custom Rust + Twemproxy + Memcached system to do it. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) AI / LLM cost explosion — every gateway in 2025-2026 is being retrofitted with per-customer token counters and per-virtual-key budgets because uncapped LLM passthrough has produced public bill-shock incidents; this is the single biggest 'why now'. 2) Usage-based billing has gone mainstream (Stripe Meters GA, OpenMeter and Lago rapid growth, Snowflake / Datadog public pricing-model debates) — every B2B SaaS launching in 2025-2026 needs a real-time per-customer meter. 3) DDoS / scraping pressure from AI training crawlers (Common Crawl / Bytespider / GPTBot / Perplexity) drove explicit edge rate-limit launches at Cloudflare, Fastly and Netlify in 2024-2025. 4) Cloudflare Workers Rate Limiting GA in September 2025 and Fastly's Edge Rate Limiting public-preview / GA timeline make 'edge-native rate limit' a competitive-feature checkbox that smaller platforms now have to match. 5) Open-source / build-vs-buy pull — Gubernator and Envoy Rate Limit are both Apache-2.0 but neither natively ships the usage-meter side; a single-binary that does both is a real gap.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: GDPR / CCPA on the customer-data side (api_key, ip and customer_id can be personal data — argues for short TTLs on IP-keyed state, hashed customer IDs and EU-region-pinning). PCI-DSS for payment-adjacent gateways that meter usage tied to payment events. SOC2 for any platform selling rate-limit-as-a-service. SOX and ASC 606 / IFRS 15 revenue-recognition rules on the billing-counter side — undercount means revenue leak, overcount means refund liability, both auditable. Crucially, beava's v0 lack of TLS / auth on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 is a hard blocker — no edge / CDN / multi-tenant gateway team can deploy a counter-store that lacks mTLS and a per-tenant auth model. The /admin sidecar on :8090 in particular has to be locked down before any external buyer will evaluate seriously.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast for a single-binary demo: a `@bv.event Request(api_key, ts, bytes)` + `@bv.table(key=api_key)` with count_60s / count_3600s / sum_bytes_24h aggregations + a 50-line Cloudflare Worker that does `http://beava-sidecar/get(api_key)` is a 1-2 day prototype. 1-2 weeks to a useful pilot at an internal-developer-platform team that wants to consolidate ten different bespoke Lua scripts. 2-6 months to be production-grade at a public edge provider (TLS, auth, multi-tenant namespaces, cross-region async sync, billing-grade idempotency).

competition.incumbents: Redis (with redis-cell GCRA module, Lua-script sliding-window patterns, and Upstash's connectionless HTTP-Redis client which is the de-facto edge rate-limit backend for Vercel / Cloudflare / Deno / Netlify / Supabase via @upstash/ratelimit), Memcached / Twemproxy (Cloudflare's own per-PoP rate-limit counter store), Cloudflare Durable Objects (native, per-key strongly-consistent state for Workers but capped at ~500-1 k RPS per object), Aerospike (used by some tier-1 ad/gateway stacks), ScyllaDB, Hazelcast IMDG. Open-source rate-limit services: Gubernator (mailgun, Apache-2.0, gRPC, distributes counters without Redis), Envoy Rate Limit (envoyproxy, Apache-2.0, Go, Redis-backed), NVIDIA go-ratelimit (Apache-2.0, Redis-backed), Apache APISIX rate-limit plugins, Kong Rate Limiting Advanced (local + cluster + redis strategies), Tyk DRL (in-cluster distributed counter). Usage-metering side: OpenMeter (Apache-2.0, Kafka + ClickHouse, explicitly markets 'usage gating on the edge with low latency'), Lago (open-source, 'up to 1 M billing events/s'), Metronome / Orb / Schematic / Stripe Meters (commercial).
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: By edge-platform / vendor: Cloudflare native Rate Limiting API + Durable Objects (GA Sept 2025), Fastly Edge Rate Limiting + ratecounter VCL + Compute@Edge KV Store, Netlify Rate Limiting + Netlify Blobs, Vercel Edge / Edge Config + Vercel KV (Upstash-backed), Deno Deploy + Deno KV, Supabase Edge Functions + Upstash Redis pattern. By gateway: Kong Rate Limiting Advanced (Redis or local cluster), Tyk DRL, Apigee Quota policy, Apache APISIX limit-count / limit-req / limit-conn, Zuplo built-in rate-limit, AWS API Gateway Usage Plans, Azure API Management throttling. By AI gateway: Portkey, Helicone, LiteLLM, TrueFoundry, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Envoy AI Gateway, Kong AI Rate Limiting Advanced, Apache APISIX AI Rate Limiting, Azure API Management llm-token-limit. By usage-metering: OpenMeter, Lago, Metronome, Orb, Stripe Meters, Schematic.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single binary with no Kafka / Flink / Redis-cluster ceremony — the entire incumbent landscape is two-tier (gateway + external Redis/ClickHouse). 2) 50+ aggregation primitives (count, velocity, sum, distribution, n_unique, recency) cover BOTH the rate-limit side and the usage-meter side in one engine — today buyers use Redis-cell for rate limit AND a separate Kafka + ClickHouse stack (OpenMeter) for the meter. 3) Sub-ms TCP + msgpack matches inline edge latency budget without HTTP overhead — Upstash's HTTP-Redis client is connectionless but adds milliseconds; beava's framed-TCP shaves that out. 4) Apache-2.0, no open-core (unlike Redis post-RSAL / Aerospike / Kong Enterprise / Tyk Pro). 5) Per-event push-and-track model (the bidder / edge-worker already produces per-request events; just push them) — much less plumbing than 'EVAL a Lua script on every request'. 6) Built-in window semantics (sliding / tumbling / hopping) rather than rolling-your-own Lua + ZSET trick. 7) Refuse-on-network-FS / WAL-on-local-NVMe is exactly the discipline you want in a per-PoP sidecar — same posture as the bespoke Rust services Cloudflare and AWS API Gateway already run internally.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth on any wire surface — disqualifying for any production edge / CDN / API-gateway deployment because the rate-limit sidecar inevitably exposes :8081 / :8090 to co-tenants. 2) No multi-tenancy primitives (per-tenant namespaces, per-tenant quotas on memory / writes, per-tenant rate-limit on the admin surface) — a PaaS running beava for many customers can't isolate them. 3) No cross-region async-sync of counters — Cloudflare's blog and Tyk's DRL design both acknowledge eventual consistency, but at least they ship the convergence; beava v0 does not. 4) No billing-grade idempotency-by-event-id primitive — usage meters that feed invoices need it; OpenMeter / Lago ship Kafka-based dedup. 5) No triggers / 'fire when counter crosses threshold' — limits-as-an-action (return 429, dial down quota) is what every gateway wants; today the gateway has to poll. 6) No native integration with the major edge runtimes — Cloudflare Workers and Vercel Edge cannot speak framed TCP (network is HTTP-only outside Durable Objects); HTTP/JSON works but is slower. 7) In-memory only with WAL+snapshot — billing-grade durability needs a documented cold-start replay-time SLA for tens-of-GB hot meter state, which beava has not published. 8) No native PromQL / OpenTelemetry export for the operator-facing rate-limit metrics that gateway buyers expect out of the box. 9) No reference adapter for OpenMeter / Lago / Stripe Meters event-format (CloudEvents). 10) v0 has no public edge / gateway case study — Upstash + Cloudflare and Cloudflare Durable Objects both have public production users.
competition.integration_surface: Producers: edge worker / function (Cloudflare Worker, Fastly Compute, Netlify / Vercel / Deno / Supabase edge function, Bun edge) emitting per-request events via HTTP/JSON :8080 or — for non-edge gateway sidecars — framed TCP+msgpack :8081; API gateway plugin (Kong / APISIX / Envoy filter / Tyk middleware) emitting after-request hooks; AI-gateway worker emitting token-usage events. Consumers: the same gateway / worker reading `get(api_key)` on the next request; the usage-billing pipeline (OpenMeter Kafka ingest, Lago HTTP ingest, Stripe Meters reporting API) reading aggregated counters at minute / hour cadence; observability (Prometheus / Grafana, Datadog, OpenTelemetry collectors) pulling metrics. Notably the major edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge) restrict outbound to HTTP / fetch, so the framed-TCP advantage only applies to gateway sidecars and self-hosted edge runtimes (Deno self-host, Supabase self-host, Fastly Compute non-runtime contexts).
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both, but mostly rules. Rate-limit / quota enforcement is a deterministic threshold rule (count >= cap => 429, token_bucket_remaining <= 0 => 429) read directly from beava. ML scoring shows up only on the abuse-detection side (Castle / Arkose-style bot scoring, Cloudflare Bot Fight Mode) where beava's per-IP velocity / distribution features feed an external scorer (XGBoost / ONNX in a sidecar). Billing-side is pure aggregation, no scoring.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public beava users in this domain yet. [uncertain] Comparable production systems: Cloudflare's own per-PoP rate-limit counter (Rust + Twemproxy + Memcached, public blog 'Counting Things — a lot of different things'); Fastly Edge Rate Limiting (production GA with ratecounter VCL at 200 k entries / site); Netlify Rate Limiting (production GA, IP-and-domain aggregator); Cloudflare Workers Rate Limiting (GA Sept 2025); @upstash/ratelimit (the de-facto serverless rate-limit library, used across Vercel / Cloudflare / Deno / Netlify / Supabase ecosystems); Stripe Rate Limits (public docs); AWS API Gateway Usage Plans (public default 10 k RPS); OpenMeter customers (Trigger.dev is publicly named for 'per-millisecond compute billing'); Lago (public-claim '1 M billing events/s'); AI-gateway public users (Portkey / Helicone / LiteLLM customer lists). Open-source projects that could be plumbed onto beava: Gubernator, Envoy Rate Limit, NVIDIA go-ratelimit, OpenMeter (as a downstream sink), Lago.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion threads on edge / CDN / gateway rate-limit use cases identified in this snapshot. [uncertain] Adjacent active community: Cloudflare blog series on rate limiting (multiple 2017-2025 posts), Cloudflare changelog Sept-2025 'Rate Limiting in Workers is now GA', Fastly's 'Advanced Rate Limiting on Fastly's Edge' blog, Upstash blog 'Edge Rate Limiting' and 'Serverless Rate Limiting', Netlify developer-blog rate-limit guides, multiple Dev.to / Medium articles on token-bucket / sliding-window / GCRA, Hacker News threads on Durable Objects vs Upstash for rate limiting, github.com/upstash/ratelimit-js issues and discussion, github.com/mailgun/gubernator, github.com/envoyproxy/ratelimit, github.com/brandur/redis-cell, AI-gateway category posts on TrueFoundry / Portkey / Helicone / LiteLLM blogs in 2024-2026, OpenMeter Slack / GitHub community.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No edge / rate-limit / usage-meter vertical demo identified in beava/python/beava/demos/ as of this snapshot. [uncertain] The closest existing demo is the adtech frequency-capping demo (events.jsonl + Impression / Click / Conversion schema) which exercises the same primitive (counter + window per composite key). A dedicated `examples/edge-rate-limit/` or `examples/usage-metering/` with a mock Cloudflare-Worker / Express / FastAPI gateway pushing per-request events and reading back token-bucket state is a one-afternoon authoring task that would directly demonstrate this use case.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Mixed. The rate-limit / billing-meter dimensions are passive-load — clients are honest API consumers, not adversaries. The DDoS / scraping / bot-traffic dimension layered on top IS actively adversarial (AI-training crawlers, credential-stuffing botnets, scraper bots), but the adversary is attacking the origin, not the counter itself; the counter just has to keep up with the load and not lose accuracy when the IP cardinality explodes. Feature drift is slow — token-bucket and sliding-window have been stable primitives for 30 years. The pressure is operational (cold-start, eviction policy under cardinality explosion) rather than adversarial.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Acting as the edge worker / function runtime itself — beava is the counter-store sidecar, not Cloudflare Workers or Deno Deploy. 2) Acting as the WAF / bot-detection ML model — that's Cloudflare Bot Fight Mode / Castle / Arkose; beava feeds them. 3) Acting as the billing system of record — Stripe / OpenMeter / Lago / Metronome are the invoicing systems; beava feeds them. 4) Cross-region strongly-consistent global counters — beava v0 cannot do this and the incumbent edge platforms (Cloudflare, Fastly, Tyk DRL) explicitly accept eventual consistency. 5) Long-historical lookback over months of per-request events — that's ClickHouse / BigQuery / Parquet territory. 6) Cross-customer joins ('which API keys share an IP') — that's a graph / OLAP problem. 7) Acting as Durable Objects' actor-model substitute — beava is per-key state but does not run user code per-key. 8) Replacing CDN cache / KV-store semantics (Workers KV, Fastly KV, Deno KV) — those are read-heavy bulk-key blobs; beava is write-heavy small-counter cells.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) TLS termination and mutual-TLS on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 plus a token / mTLS auth model — without this, no edge / CDN / multi-tenant gateway operator can deploy beava in their stack. 2) Multi-tenant namespaces with per-tenant memory and write quotas plus per-tenant rate-limit on the beava admin surface itself, so a single beava cluster can safely serve many customer domains. 3) First-class idempotency / dedup-by-event-id primitive so the same per-request event from a retried-on-failure edge worker is counted exactly once on the billing meter side (OpenMeter, Lago and Stripe Meters all key dedup by event-id). 4) Async cross-region / cross-PoP counter sync (CRDT-style G-Counter or log-shipping) so per-PoP counters converge to a global view; Cloudflare's blog and Tyk DRL describe exactly this pattern. 5) Triggers / 'fire when counter crosses threshold' so the gateway can install a 'return 429 when count > cap' callback rather than poll. 6) Eviction primitives on IP-keyed dimensions (Fastly's 200 k-entries-per-site LRU cap is the model) so cardinality explosion under DDoS does not OOM the box. 7) Per-key TTL with explicit window semantics tied to billing-timezone midnight resets and to billing-period boundaries (month-aligned tumbling). 8) Native Cloudflare Workers / Vercel Edge / Deno KV adapter — these runtimes are HTTP-only on outbound, so a thin HTTP-shim that batches multiple counter ops into one request is required to make beava-from-Worker viable. 9) Native OpenTelemetry / Prometheus metric export for operator-facing rate-limit dashboards (Datadog / Grafana). 10) Reference adapter for OpenMeter / Lago / Stripe Meters CloudEvents event-format so beava aggregations can sink directly into the billing pipeline. 11) Documented and benchmarked cold-start WAL-replay time for 10-100 GB hot counter state with stated SLO for time-to-first-correct-counter post-restart. 12) An `examples/edge-rate-limit/` and `examples/usage-metering/` vertical demo (a mock Worker / gateway + beava sidecar + a 5-min docker-compose).
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes for two of the three sub-domains. Rate-limit enforcement needs trigger-action ('when count >= cap, return 429' or 'when token-bucket empty, signal back-pressure to the caller'); today the gateway polls beava on every request, which is fine on the read path but wasteful for the cap-breach-alerting / quota-exhausted notification path. Usage metering needs trigger-action for budget alerts and hard kill-switches ('when monthly_token_spend > $X, suspend customer's virtual_key'); Stripe-style billing systems already expose this and the buyer expects it from a counter-store too. Abuse / DDoS needs trigger-action ('when ip_velocity_60s > N, push ip to penalty-box' — Fastly's penalty-box pattern). Pure billing-meter reads do NOT need triggers, they need clean periodic export.
